name: Ultherapy / HIFU skin tightening

angle.text: Users have this clinic treatment to lift loose skin under the chin, along the jawline and on the brow, aiming for a sharper lower-face contour without surgery. Results appear gradually over a few months. Support comes from small device studies and regulatory clearance for brow, neck and chest lifting.

summary: Clinic ultrasound device cleared for brow, neck and chest lifting; modest, gradual results and mostly small device studies.
note: Results are reported to last 1 to 2 years; burns and fat atrophy are rare reported events.
currentQuick:
Ultherapy uses focused ultrasound to heat deep skin layers so that skin looks lifted over the following months. It was first FDA cleared in 2009 for brow lifting, later for the neck, chin and chest.
Studies are mostly small device trials; reported improvement is gradual and typically lasts one to two years.
How it works: Focused ultrasound creates tiny heat zones in the dermis and SMAS layer with imaging guidance, said to prompt new collagen and elastin over time.
Risks and caveats: Common effects are redness, swelling, pain and tingling. Rarer reports include bruising, numbness, temporary facial weakness, burns and fat atrophy. It is done by trained clinicians.
deepLead:
Ultherapy is a non-invasive cosmetic procedure that uses micro-focused ultrasound with visualization (MFU-V) to heat deep skin layers, with the aim of lifting and tightening skin on areas such as the brow, neck and under the chin. It is made by Ulthera, Inc., which Merz Aesthetics acquired in 2014. Other devices using high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) for skin tightening are sold under different names.
The device received its first FDA clearance in 2009 for non-invasive eyebrow lifting, with later clearances for the neck and under-chin area in 2012 and for lines and wrinkles on the decolletage in 2014.
Evidence for skin tightening comes mainly from small device trials. One summary of pooled data reports investigator-rated improvement of about 92 percent at 90 days, while patient-reported satisfaction ranged from roughly 42 to 59 percent. Note that source itself relies partly on clinic and manufacturer material.

name: Thermage / monopolar RF

angle.text: Thermage is used in clinics to tighten mild-to-moderate skin laxity on the face, neck and eyelids, so skin looks firmer and fine lines look softer. Gradual results are reported in small studies, which is where the evidence for this appearance use currently sits.

summary: Clinic radiofrequency heating for mild-to-moderate skin laxity; small studies report modest improvement.
note: Evidence is mostly small device studies; pain and, rarely, fat loss or scarring are reported.
currentQuick:
Thermage is a clinic treatment that uses monopolar radiofrequency to heat the dermis while cooling the surface, aiming to tighten loose skin on the face, neck and eyelids.
Early studies reported improvements in wrinkle and laxity scores after a single session. Evidence is mostly small device studies.
How it works: RF energy heats deep skin, said to stimulate collagen and elastin and remodel tissue.
Risks and caveats: Pain that sometimes required sedation, skin dents, and rare fat necrosis or scarring have been reported. It is delivered by trained clinicians.
deepLead:
Thermage is a brand of non-ablative monopolar radiofrequency (RF) treatment used in clinics for skin tightening of the face, neck and eyelids. It heats the dermis with RF energy while the surface is cooled, with the aim of tightening lax skin and softening fine lines without surgery. The device was first sold as ThermaCool and is now marketed as Thermage FLX.
RF skin tightening in general is described as heating the dermis to stimulate collagen, elastin and hyaluronic acid production and tissue remodelling, with a dermal target temperature of about 67 degrees C cited. Early studies from 2003 to 2004 reported improvement in periorbital and cheek or neck laxity after single treatments.
Published studies are mostly small and company-linked device studies, and sources note adverse effects including pain and, rarely, fat loss or scarring.

name: Profhilo / skin booster injectables

angle.text: Profhilo and similar skin boosters are used to improve skin quality, giving a more hydrated, supple and smoother-looking complexion rather than added volume. Small studies report gains in hydration and elasticity, and the products are generally positioned as complements to fillers.

summary: Injectable hyaluronic acid sold as skin bio-remodelling; small studies report better hydration and elasticity, not volume.
note: Not FDA-approved per a January 2026 source; evidence is mostly small open-label studies.
currentQuick:
Profhilo is an injectable hyaluronic acid made by IBSA and sold in Europe since 2015. It is meant to improve skin quality, hydration and elasticity rather than add volume, and belongs to the wider 'skin booster' category.
Evidence is mostly small open-label studies and post-marketing safety data.
How it works: It combines high and low molecular weight HA, proposed to stimulate fibroblasts to produce collagen and elastin and to hydrate the dermis.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects are mostly minor: swelling, redness, bruising. HA injectables can rarely cause vascular occlusion. A source states it was not FDA-approved as of January 2026.
deepLead:
Profhilo is an injectable hyaluronic acid (HA) product made by IBSA Derma, launched in Europe in 2015, that is marketed as a skin 'bio-remodelling' treatment rather than a volume filler. Each syringe combines high and low molecular weight HA stabilised by a heat process, with no chemical cross-linker.
It belongs to a broader category called skin boosters: injectables placed in the dermis to improve hydration, elasticity and texture instead of adding volume. A 2024 review traces how the term evolved from HA fillers and notes that definitions of the category vary.
Evidence consists mainly of small open-label studies and post-marketing data. As of January 2026, one source states that Profhilo was not FDA-approved in the US.

name: Rejuran / salmon DNA facial

angle.text: Rejuran and other salmon DNA (PN or PDRN) facials are promoted for skin texture, fine lines and under-eye skin quality, as an alternative to volume fillers. Popularity has run ahead of published data, and the evidence for this appearance use is still thin.

summary: Polynucleotide (PN) skin-booster injections made from salmon DNA, sold as a skin-quality treatment; evidence for appearance use is still thin and mostly unpublished.
note: Clinic-administered injectable; public sources describe few published controlled trials, and the registered trials found are comparisons or not yet recruiting.
currentQuick:
A salmon DNA facial is a cosmetic injection treatment in which fragments of fish-derived DNA (polynucleotides, sometimes called PDRN) are placed into the skin by a clinician. Rejuran is the best-known brand. It is marketed for skin texture, fine lines, under-eye skin and general skin quality rather than for filling volume.
It entered looksmaxxing discussion as one of several injectable 'skin booster' options, grouped with other hardmaxx procedures. Registered trials exist for crow's feet and for periorbital and neck uses, but the sources found describe few published, controlled results.
How it works: Proponents and aesthetic-medicine sources say the polynucleotides stimulate fibroblast activity and collagen production and support tissue repair, and that the injection also hydrates and conditions the skin. Public encyclopedia summaries describe this as a proposed mechanism from recent studies rather than an established one.
Risks and caveats: Common reported effects of skin-booster injections in general are temporary redness, swelling and bruising at injection sites; as with any injection, infection and allergic reaction are possible. One general source notes that therapeutic polynucleotides can trigger immune activation. Regulation of PN products varies by country, and the sources reviewed give no skin-specific safety dataset.
deepLead:
A Rejuran or salmon DNA facial is a cosmetic procedure in which a polynucleotide (PN) preparation, derived from salmon DNA, is injected into or just beneath the skin to improve its quality. The best-known product name is Rejuran, and the ingredient is also referred to as polydeoxyribonucleotide (PDRN). It is promoted for skin texture, fine lines, under-eye skin and overall rejuvenation rather than for adding volume the way a conventional filler does.
Aesthetic-medicine descriptions say the material is thought to stimulate fibroblast activity and collagen production and to promote tissue regeneration, and report improved elasticity and reduced wrinkles after subcutaneous injection; the encyclopedia summaries do not describe the size or design of the underlying studies. Wikipedia notes that fish-derived polynucleotide is used in aesthetic medicine as a dermal filler.
Several clinical trials involving PN-type products have been registered, including non-inferiority and comparison studies for crow's feet lines and not-yet-recruiting studies of periorbital hollowing and horizontal neck lines. In looksmaxxing communities the treatment is discussed as a skin-quality or under-eye option among injectables.

name: PRP facial (vampire facial)

chain: Better texture, fewer fine lines and scars
angle.text: Users have PRP facials, popularly the vampire facial, for rejuvenated skin, smoother texture, fine lines and acne scars. Some do-it-yourself communities also try home versions. Small studies exist for skin rejuvenation, though controlled evidence for facial appearance is limited.

summary: Microneedling combined with your own platelet-rich plasma, popularised as the 'vampire facial'; controlled evidence for facial rejuvenation is limited and infection control is the main safety issue.
note: In 2024 the CDC reported HIV infections linked to vampire facials at an unlicensed New Mexico spa, after a state warning in 2018.
currentQuick:
A PRP facial uses a small sample of the person's own blood, spun in a centrifuge to concentrate platelets, which is then applied to the skin, usually during microneedling. The press nicknamed it the 'vampire facial' and celebrity endorsements made it widely known in the 2010s.
It is marketed for skin texture, fine lines and glow. Reviews describe the wider evidence for PRP as mixed across conditions, and the facial use itself has limited controlled data. Some looksmaxxing forum members have discussed doing PRP at home as part of a larger regimen.
How it works: PRP contains platelets and growth factors that proponents say signal skin cells to repair tissue and build collagen, while the microneedling creates controlled micro-injuries that start a healing response. The sources reviewed do not describe a settled mechanism for facial skin.
Risks and caveats: Reported side effects include redness, swelling, bruising and numbness, usually resolving within days. The main safety concern described by health authorities is infection from unlicensed providers who reuse or inadequately sterilise equipment; in 2024 the CDC reported three HIV diagnoses linked to a New Mexico spa. In the US the FDA does not regulate PRP itself, though the devices used to prepare it require clearance.
deepLead:
A PRP facial, popularly known as a vampire facial, is a cosmetic procedure in which blood drawn from the patient is centrifuged to produce platelet-rich plasma (PRP), which is then applied to the face, most often together with microneedling. It is marketed for skin rejuvenation, fine lines, texture and acne scars.
PRP is a concentrate of plasma from a person's own blood with red blood cells removed and platelets kept, usually raised to about three to five times normal levels. Its evidence base is described as mixed: it appears to help in some conditions and not in others, and facial rejuvenation is one of several aesthetic uses with limited support. Side effects such as redness, swelling and bruising are typically brief.
The main documented harm is infection transmission when procedures are performed by unlicensed operators. New Mexico health officials warned in 2018 about a business offering vampire facials, and in 2024 the CDC reported that three women had been diagnosed with HIV after treatments at an Albuquerque spa. The treatment has also been discussed in looksmaxxing forums, including by members who describe doing PRP microneedling themselves.

name: Mesotherapy

chain: Local effect on skin, hair or fat
Fuller hair, fresher skin, less fat
angle.text: Mesotherapy is used to inject vitamin and drug cocktails for hair thickening, skin rejuvenation and local fat reduction. Small studies back some uses, such as scalp treatment, while cocktails vary widely and appearance claims for fat and skin remain largely untested.

summary: Cocktail micro-injections into the skin, used for hair, skin and fat; supported by small studies in some uses, with limited standardisation and documented infection outbreaks from poor hygiene.
note: Ingredients vary by practitioner; infections including atypical mycobacteria have been reported after non-sterile procedures.
currentQuick:
Mesotherapy means injecting small amounts of medications, vitamins, hyaluronic acid or other substances into the skin or just beneath it with fine needles. It was developed in France in 1952 by Michel Pistor, initially for pain, and later spread to cosmetic uses such as skin rejuvenation, hair loss and localised fat.
In looksmaxxing forums the term most often comes up for scalp mesotherapy alongside finasteride, dutasteride or minoxidil. Evidence is described as limited by small studies and non-standard mixtures, and expert bodies have not endorsed cosmetic fat removal.
How it works: Proponents say microinjections create a local depot that diffuses slowly, giving higher local concentrations with lower doses, and that the needle trauma itself stimulates repair. Reviews and critics note that the mixtures differ widely and that, for fat reduction, any effect may come from tissue damage by detergent-like ingredients.
Risks and caveats: Reported harms include injection-site infections, allergic reactions, tissue damage and inflammation. Outbreaks of rapidly growing mycobacteria followed mesotherapy and surgery in Brazil, and Australian clients developed abscesses. In the US the FDA cannot control what practitioners inject and state boards oversee the practice; only deoxycholic acid (Kybella) is approved for submental fat, and some countries restrict or ban cosmetic uses.
deepLead:
Mesotherapy, also called local intradermal therapy, is a technique in which small doses of drugs, vitamins, minerals, enzymes, hyaluronic acid or plant extracts are injected through fine needles into the dermis or just beneath the skin. Its stated aim is localised action with minimal systemic exposure. A needle-free pressurised version delivers the ingredients with a jet of air.
French physician Michel Pistor is credited with developing it in 1952, initially using procaine injections for pain and vascular disorders; the term mesotherapy dates to 1958 and the French Academy of Medicine recognised it as a medical specialty in 1987. Cosmetic uses developed later and include skin rejuvenation, hair loss and localised fat and cellulite treatment, and phosphatidylcholine injections for fat gained attention in Brazil and the United States.
The scientific record is mixed. Small trials and reviews report benefit in some pain and hair-loss settings, while Wikipedia states that cosmetic uses have generally not been tested in standard clinical trials, and reviews cite small samples and unstandardised mixtures. Infection outbreaks have followed non-sterile practice. In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed mainly for hair loss alongside drug regimens.

name: IPL photofacial

chain: Light pulses target pigment and vessels
angle.text: IPL photofacials are used to fade sun spots, uneven pigmentation, redness and visible small blood vessels for a clearer, more even complexion. Support is strongest for pigment and vascular concerns, and weaker for wrinkles.

summary: Broad-spectrum light flashes used to treat sun spots, redness and broken capillaries; supported for pigment and vascular concerns, less so for wrinkles.
note: Hyperpigmentation and burns are the main reported complications; darker skin tones carry higher risk and manufacturers advise use mainly on light to medium skin.
currentQuick:
An IPL photofacial uses a handheld device that emits short pulses of broad-spectrum light to treat visible skin problems such as sun spots, freckles, redness and small surface blood vessels. Pigment and haemoglobin in the skin absorb the light, heat up and are cleared by the body.
It is a mainstream dermatology and aesthetic treatment rather than a looksmaxxing invention. Reviews describe it as working well for pigmentation and vascular lesions and less well for wrinkles, and home devices are also sold.
How it works: A flashlamp produces light of roughly 400 to 1200 nm, with filters removing unwanted ultraviolet and long infrared wavelengths. Melanin, haemoglobin and water absorb the energy and convert it to heat, which damages the targeted pigment or vessel while a cooling system protects the skin surface.
Risks and caveats: Complications reported include hyperpigmentation, temporary redness and microscopic thermal injury; photosensitising medications and existing skin damage are listed as contraindications. A manufacturer cited in one encyclopedia entry recommends use mainly on light to medium skin tones. Regulation varies by country, and a distinction between beauty-grade and medical-grade devices is used in some places.
deepLead:
An IPL photofacial, also called photorejuvenation, is a cosmetic and dermatological treatment that uses intense pulsed light (IPL) to improve skin affected by sun damage, uneven pigmentation, redness and visible small blood vessels. A computer-controlled handheld flashlamp emits brief pulses of non-coherent, broad-spectrum light, roughly 400 to 1200 nm, which targets melanin, haemoglobin and water in the skin.
Unlike lasers, which emit a single wavelength, IPL devices use interchangeable filters so that one machine can be used for several conditions. The technology was invented by Shimon Eckhouse in 1992, and the US FDA cleared it for vascular lesions in 1995, pigmented lesions in 1996 and hair removal in 1997.
Reviews of photorejuvenation methods describe IPL as working well for pigmentation and blood-vessel lesions but less well for wrinkles, with limited or anecdotal safety data in places.

name: Plasma pen (fibroblasting)

angle.text: Plasma pens are promoted for tightening loose eyelid skin, smoothing lines and removing small blemishes, with cheaper home devices sold as clinic substitutes. Controlled trials for cosmetic tightening were not found, so the appearance benefit rests on provider and user reports.

summary: A handheld device that arcs ionised gas onto the skin, marketed for eyelid and skin tightening; no controlled trials for cosmetic tightening were found.
note: Cosmetic skin-tightening claims lack published trials in the sources reviewed; online forum posts describe home use on the eyelids.
currentQuick:
A plasma pen is a small handheld device that produces a tiny electrical arc of ionised gas between its tip and the skin. In cosmetic use it is marketed as 'fibroblasting' for tightening sagging or hooded eyelids, smoothing lines and removing small skin lesions without cutting.
It appears in looksmaxxing forums as a cheap alternative to eyelid surgery, with posts pointing to inexpensive consumer devices and much costlier clinic treatments. The sources reviewed contain no controlled trials of the cosmetic tightening claim.
How it works: Proponents say the arc heats tiny points of the skin surface, producing small controlled injuries that prompt a repair response by fibroblasts and tighten the area; this explanation was not found in published studies. Scientific literature on 'plasma pens' mainly covers cold atmospheric plasma used for disinfection and wound research, which is a different application from cosmetic burning.
Risks and caveats: Because the cosmetic method works by creating small burns, no cosmetic safety trial was found, so rates of complications are unknown from the sources reviewed. A 2025 case report describes plasma pen ablation used clinically for extensive periocular xanthogranuloma.
deepLead:
A plasma pen is a handheld device that generates a small electrical arc of ionised gas, or plasma, between its tip and the skin. Marketed in cosmetics as fibroblasting or a plasma lift, it is promoted for tightening loose skin, particularly on the eyelids, and for smoothing lines and removing small blemishes.
Plasma itself is described as the fourth state of matter, and non-thermal or cold atmospheric plasma has been studied for disinfection, wound care and dentistry. Those studies concern antimicrobial and biomedical effects in the lab and clinic and are distinct from the cosmetic technique of applying hot plasma arcs to skin to tighten it.
In looksmaxxing forums the plasma pen is presented as a low-cost route to improved eyelids and skin, with users quoting device prices and comparing them with clinic fees. The sources reviewed contain no controlled trials of cosmetic skin tightening with these devices.

name: Platysma Botox (Nefertiti lift)

chain: Less downward pull on lower face
angle.text: Users have botulinum toxin injected along the jawline and neck bands to soften platysmal cords and give a subtle lift and sharper lower-face contour. Case series and small trials describe the effect, which is temporary and modest.

summary: Botulinum toxin injected along the jawline and neck bands to soften platysmal cords and sharpen the lower-face contour; described in published case series and small trials, with temporary, modest results.
note: Effects are temporary (Grokipedia gives three to four months) and the procedure is described as suiting mild to moderate neck aging rather than severe laxity.
currentQuick:
Platysma Botox, popularly called the Nefertiti lift, is a non-surgical injection of botulinum toxin into the platysma muscle, the thin muscle sheet of the front of the neck, and along the lower border of the jaw. It aims to soften vertical neck bands and give a subtle lift and more defined jawline.
It was described in 2007 by a Swiss dermatologist, Phillip M. Levy, in a paper based on 130 patients. Later clinical studies in plastic surgery journals have examined it, including small trials comparing it with other injection patterns.
How it works: The platysma runs from the upper chest to the lower jaw and pulls the lower face and mouth corners downward when it contracts. Botulinum toxin weakens the muscle, which proponents say reduces the downward pull on the jawline and relaxes visible bands.
Risks and caveats: Published descriptions treat the procedure as minimally invasive with temporary effects that fade after a few months and need repeat sessions. Possible effects of neck toxin injections generally include bruising and weakness of neighbouring muscles; results are described as subtle compared with surgical platysmaplasty. It is clinician-administered and not specific to looksmaxxing.
deepLead:
The Nefertiti lift is a non-surgical cosmetic procedure in which botulinum toxin type A is injected into the platysma muscle, including vertical neck bands and the lower border of the mandible, to relax the muscle and reduce its downward pull on the lower face. It aims to soften platysmal bands and produce a subtle lift and sharper definition of the jawline.
The technique takes its name from the ancient Egyptian queen Nefertiti, whose bust is admired for its elongated neck and defined jaw. Swiss dermatologist Phillip M. Levy described it in the Journal of Cosmetic and Laser Therapy in 2007, reporting experience with 130 patients treated between November 2006 and April 2007.
Later studies have examined it clinically. A 2017 study injected abobotulinumtoxinA along the mandibular border and platysmal bands and examined which patients respond, and a 2018 crossover study compared the microbotox technique with the Nefertiti lift. A 2026 split-face study in The Laryngoscope evaluates its effect on jawline contour. Grokipedia describes the effects as temporary and subtle, lasting around three to four months, and best suited to mild to moderate neck aging rather than severe laxity.

name: Facial cupping

chain: Light suction moves skin and fluid
angle.text: Facial cupping is a self-care ritual in which small suction cups are glided over the face to lift, tone and depuff. People report a temporary flushed, fresher look. Face-specific research is nearly absent, so lasting lifting remains a belief.

summary: Small suction cups glided over the face to lift and depuff; popular as a self-care ritual, with almost no face-specific research behind it.
note: Can cause bruising or marks; the NCCIH warns cupping may worsen eczema or psoriasis.
currentQuick:
Facial cupping adapts traditional cupping therapy to the face, using small cups with light suction to draw skin upward. It is promoted for lifting, depuffing and brightening.
No controlled trial has tested whether it changes sagging or wrinkles. General reviews of cupping rate the evidence for claimed benefits as weak.
How it works: Suction draws skin and tissue into the cup, which proponents say boosts circulation and loosens tension. A small imaging study found measurable short-term changes in the skin's blood microenvironment during facial cupping; lasting effects have not been studied.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects of cupping include temporary marks, bruising, burns (with fire cupping), and flares of eczema or psoriasis. It is generally considered low-risk with a trained practitioner, but is not suitable for everyone.
deepLead:
Facial cupping is the application of small suction cups to the skin of the face, usually with a light, gliding or brief-hold technique, with the aim of improving circulation, lifting or toning the skin, or reducing the appearance of sagging and puffiness. It is an area-based variant of cupping therapy, a traditional practice in which suction draws skin and soft tissue into a cup .
Proponents present it as a non-invasive route to a firmer, brighter face. Published research on the face specifically is very limited: a small laboratory imaging study has measured short-term changes in skin blood vessels after facial cupping, but no controlled trial has tested whether it reduces sagging or wrinkles . Reviews of cupping in general describe the evidence for claimed health benefits as weak and of low quality .

name: Face taping (Frownies / sleep patches)

angle.text: Users wear paper or tape patches overnight on the forehead, between the brows and around the eyes and mouth to soften expression lines. Frownies has sold them for over a century. Published trials are absent, so the benefit rests on anecdote.

summary: Paper or tape patches worn overnight to hold expression lines flat; a 130-year-old idea with no published trials.
note: Brand history is company-sourced; adhesive can irritate sensitive skin.
currentQuick:
Face taping means sticking patches over expression lines such as forehead and frown lines, typically overnight. Frownies, a brand dating to 1889 by its own account, is the best-known version.
Proponents say keeping the skin and muscles still softens lines over time. No published trial has tested this.
How it works: The patch is a stiff splint that holds skin flat and limits muscle creasing while worn. There is no active ingredient, and the maker says any effect is temporary.
Risks and caveats: No safety studies were found. As with any adhesive on the skin, irritation is possible; products are sold as cosmetics rather than medical devices.
deepLead:
Face taping is the practice of applying adhesive patches or tape to areas of expression lines, such as the forehead, the vertical lines between the eyebrows and the corners of the eyes and mouth, usually overnight, to hold the skin flat and discourage the underlying muscles from creasing it. The best-known product is Frownies, an American brand of paper patches with a water-activated adhesive .
Proponents say that holding the skin smooth and limiting muscle movement while it is worn can soften expression lines over weeks or months of consistent use. The manufacturer describes the effect as temporary and dependent on ongoing use . No clinical trial of face-taping patches was found in the sources reviewed, and the claim that overnight taping reduces wrinkles has not been tested in published studies.

name: Lymphatic drainage facial massage

angle.text: Users massage the face and neck lightly, by hand or with tools, to reduce puffiness and get a more defined, depuffed look. The manual technique is established in clinical settings, while cosmetic facial evidence is absent.

summary: Gentle face and neck massage meant to depuff; the technique is real, but cosmetic facial evidence is absent.
note: Evidence for MLD is in lymphedema, not facial cosmetic use.
currentQuick:
Lymphatic drainage facial massage uses very light strokes on the face and neck to encourage fluid movement, with the aim of reducing puffiness.
The parent technique, manual lymphatic drainage, dates to 1930s Europe and is studied for lymphedema with mixed results. Facial cosmetic use has not been studied.
How it works: Proponents say light rhythmic pressure helps lymph flow away from swollen tissue. Light-pressure MLD is the technique reported in the lymphedema literature.
Risks and caveats: No facial-specific safety data were found. The sources reviewed do not discuss contraindications.
deepLead:
Lymphatic drainage facial massage is a light, rhythmic, hands-on or tool-assisted massage of the face and neck intended to move lymph fluid, with the aim of reducing puffiness and giving a more defined, 'depuffed' appearance. It draws on manual lymphatic drainage (MLD), a gentle skin technique developed in the 1930s .
Proponents promote it for reducing facial swelling and improving tone. The evidence base for MLD itself is centered on lymphedema and is mixed . No studies of facial lymphatic massage for cosmetic depuffing were found in the sources reviewed.

name: Topical estrogen (estriol) cream

chain: Estriol acts on skin estrogen receptors
angle.text: Estriol cream is discussed for thicker, firmer, smoother skin, mostly among older users. It is an off-label use of a menopausal hormone therapy ingredient. Skin data exist in menopausal women, while data for appearance use in general are thin.

summary: A weak estrogen cream discussed for skin thickness; menopausal skin data exist, appearance-use data are thin.
note: Hormone product; generally prescription-only, with estrogen-class effects.
currentQuick:
Estriol is a mild natural estrogen used mainly in menopausal therapy. Creams are promoted for skin thickness and collagen.
Wikipedia reports research showing it can reverse postmenopausal skin thinning; facial appearance trials in other groups were not found.
How it works: Estriol activates estrogen receptors but more weakly than estradiol, acting as a partial agonist.
Risks and caveats: Generally well tolerated; reported effects include breast tenderness and local irritation. Like other estrogens it can cause endometrial hyperplasia. It is generally prescription-only.
deepLead:
Estriol (E3) is a weak natural estrogen, one of the three major endogenous estrogens alongside estradiol and estrone, and is available as a medication mainly for menopausal hormone therapy. It is sold as tablets, vaginal creams and suppositories, and some skin creams, some over the counter and some from compounding pharmacies .
In appearance circles, estriol cream is discussed as a way to counter the decline in skin thickness and collagen after menopause. Wikipedia reports that research has found estriol can reverse the postmenopausal decline in skin thickness and collagen . The sources reviewed did not include trial details, and no appearance-specific clinical studies were summarised here.

name: Topical rapamycin

angle.text: Longevity-minded users apply rapamycin cream hoping to slow visible skin aging. It is an off-label use, since topical forms are approved for a rare facial condition. One small exploratory aging trial exists.

summary: Rapamycin creams for skin aging; approved for a rare facial condition, with only one small exploratory aging trial.
note: Prescription drug; the aging-skin evidence is a small exploratory trial.
currentQuick:
Rapamycin (sirolimus) is an mTOR inhibitor first found in Easter Island soil bacteria. Topical gel is approved for facial angiofibromas in tuberous sclerosis.
For aging skin, one small exploratory randomized trial reported reduced senescence markers; appearance outcomes are not established.
How it works: It binds FKBP12 and inhibits mTOR, a pathway linked to aging in animal research.
Risks and caveats: Oral sirolimus has serious systemic risks (infections, lipids, lung toxicity, wound healing). Topical use in trials mostly caused mild irritation. It is prescription-only.
deepLead:
Rapamycin, also called sirolimus, is a macrolide compound first isolated in 1972 from bacteria in soil samples from Easter Island (Rapa Nui). It inhibits the protein mTOR and is approved as an oral immunosuppressant for transplant patients and for the lung disease lymphangioleiomyomatosis . Topical formulations are approved for facial angiofibromas in tuberous sclerosis complex (the FDA approved a sirolimus gel in 2022 and the EU authorised Hyftor in 2023) .
In anti-aging circles, topical rapamycin is discussed as a skin-aging intervention based on mTOR's role in aging. A small exploratory randomized trial reported reduced markers of senescence in human skin . Evidence for visible appearance benefit is limited to that exploratory work.

name: Quit smoking / vaping

chain: Better skin blood flow and collagen
angle.text: Quitting tobacco or vaping is cited to avoid or reduce smoker's face, with its wrinkles, sagging and dull yellowish complexion. The link between smoking and facial aging is observational, and trials of quitting for appearance are missing.

summary: Giving up tobacco to avoid 'smoker's face'; the aging link is observational, and quitting-for-looks trials are missing.
note: Smoking's link to premature facial aging is observational.
currentQuick:
Smoking is associated with a distinctive aged look: wrinkles, sagging and a dull complexion. Quitting is discussed as a way to avoid that.
The association is documented in observational research; no trial of quitting for appearance was found, and vaping has not been studied for facial aging.
How it works: Smoking is proposed to reduce skin oxygen and antioxidants, narrow blood vessels, and break down collagen and elastin.
Risks and caveats: Quitting itself carries no appearance-specific risks in the sources reviewed; smoking is linked to many serious diseases.
deepLead:
In looksmaxxing and skincare discussions, quitting smoking or vaping is cited as a way to avoid or slow smoking-related facial aging. 'Smoker's face' is the term for facial changes seen in many long-term smokers, including a pattern of wrinkles, sagging and a dull, yellowish or grayish complexion .
Medical sources attribute these changes to reduced oxygen and nutrient supply, breakdown of the skin's structural matrix, and oxidative stress . No trials of quitting for appearance were found in the sources reviewed, and no studies of vaping and facial aging were found.

name: Sleeping on your back

angle.text: Some looksmaxxing practitioners sleep face-up to avoid sleep lines caused by pressing the face into a pillow for hours. The idea is based on anecdote and plausible mechanics, and the wrinkle benefit has not been tested in trials.

summary: Sleeping face-up to dodge pillow creases; the wrinkle benefit has not been tested in trials.
note: Position is linked to apnea and reflux in sleep research; no wrinkle trials exist.
currentQuick:
Some looksmaxxers sleep on their backs so the face is not pressed into a pillow, aiming to avoid sleep lines.
Sources note habitual sleep position is associated with wrinkles, but no study detail is given and no trial has tested changing position.
How it works: The idea is that avoiding repeated compression of facial skin overnight reduces creasing over time. This mechanism has not been tested directly.
Risks and caveats: Sleep literature links supine sleep to worse positional sleep apnea, reflux after meals and more sleep paralysis in some people. Supine sleep is not discussed as a cosmetic risk.
deepLead:
Sleeping on your back (the supine position) is a sleep posture that some looksmaxxing practitioners adopt in the belief that it avoids so-called sleep lines, the facial creases attributed to pressing the face into a pillow or mattress for hours each night.
Reference sources describe three main sleep positions in adults: lateral (on the side), supine (face up) and prone (face down). The lateral position is the most common, followed by supine and then prone. Wikipedia's article on wrinkles states that habitual sleeping positions are linked to wrinkles, citing a dermatology-society resource, but gives no study detail for the claim. No published trial has been located that tests whether changing sleep position alters facial wrinkles.

name: Bee venom / snake peptide (Syn-Ake) creams

angle.text: Syn-Ake and bee venom creams are sold as topical alternatives to Botox for smoothing expression lines. The reasoning is that a peptide mimics a venom compound and relaxes muscle. Evidence so far consists of laboratory data.

summary: Venom-mimic creams sold as topical Botox alternatives; only lab data exist.
note: Bee venom contains known allergens; no human wrinkle trials found.
currentQuick:
These creams use bee venom or the synthetic Syn-Ake peptide to promote smoother-looking skin.
Published work is limited to computer and cell-based studies; no human trials were found.
How it works: Syn-Ake is said to act on neurotransmitter signalling to relax expression lines; lab studies also tested effects on matrix metalloproteinases and antioxidant activity.
Risks and caveats: Bee venom contains allergens such as phospholipase A2. Safety data for Syn-Ake creams in humans were not found in the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
Bee venom and Syn-Ake creams are cosmetics that borrow from venoms: bee venom products use honeybee venom or its components, while Syn-Ake is a synthetic peptide marketed as a topical alternative to botulinum toxin for wrinkles, named for its design as a mimic of a snake-venom peptide.
Published work on Syn-Ake consists of laboratory and computational studies. A 2024 study used in silico docking and in vitro tests to examine interactions with matrix metalloproteinases and sirtuin 1 and measured antioxidant activity. A 2026 paper described a nanoemulsion formulation of the peptide and evaluated it in silico and in vitro. No human trials were found.

name: Sunscreen-maxxing

angle.text: Sunscreen-maxxing means strict daily SPF use with regular reapplication to limit UV-driven skin aging. It is regarded as the best-evidenced anti-photoaging habit in the wiki's sources, with studies showing less visible skin aging in regular users.

summary: Daily SPF and strict reapplication; the most evidence-backed anti-photoageing habit in the wiki's sources.
note: Allergic reactions possible; ingredient rules differ by country.
currentQuick:
Sunscreen-maxxing means wearing sunscreen daily and reapplying, mainly to prevent sun-driven skin ageing.
A randomised Australian trial reported smoother skin after 4.5 years of daily broad-spectrum use compared with usual habits.
How it works: Sunscreen filters or blocks UV radiation; SPF reflects UVB protection and broad-spectrum labels indicate UVA protection too.
Risks and caveats: Reported issues include allergic contact dermatitis and, in some aerosols, benzene contamination. Typical use is not usually linked to vitamin D deficiency. Studies find many people apply too little.
deepLead:
Sunscreen-maxxing is the looksmaxxing term for strict daily use of sunscreen, with regular reapplication, to limit ultraviolet exposure and the skin ageing attributed to it.
Sunscreens are rated by sun protection factor (SPF), introduced by Franz Greiter in 1974, which mainly reflects protection against UVB. Broad-spectrum products also protect against UVA. Reference sources report that sunscreen can help prevent melanoma and squamous cell carcinoma, and a randomised trial in Australia found that daily broad-spectrum use for 4.5 years was associated with smoother, more resilient skin than usual habits.

name: Tretinoin protocol (tret, buffering)

chain: Collagen builds, pores and spots improve
angle.text: Looksmaxxing forums share routines for starting tretinoin slowly and buffering it with moisturiser to reduce irritation, aiming for smoother, clearer, less wrinkled skin. Tretinoin itself is well studied for acne and photoaging, while the buffering routine is not.

summary: Slow-ramped, moisturiser-buffered prescription retinoid use; tretinoin itself is well studied, the buffering routine is not.
note: Prescription retinoid; contraindicated in pregnancy; causes irritation and sun sensitivity.
currentQuick:
The tret protocol is community shorthand for easing into prescription tretinoin and cushioning it with moisturiser.
Tretinoin is the most studied topical retinoid for photoageing; no studies were found on buffering specifically.
How it works: Tretinoin acts on retinoic acid receptors in skin cells, normalising follicle keratinisation and, per reports, boosting collagen. Buffering is meant to reduce irritation, not change the mechanism.
Risks and caveats: Irritation, redness, peeling and sun sensitivity are common. It is contraindicated in pregnancy. It is available by prescription in many countries.
deepLead:
The tretinoin protocol, often shortened to "tret" in forums, refers to the way looksmaxxing practitioners introduce and use topical tretinoin, a prescription retinoid, typically by increasing use slowly and sometimes "buffering" it with moisturiser to reduce irritation.
Topical tretinoin is described as the most extensively studied retinoid for photoageing, and studies have run up to two years. Its common adverse effects are irritation, redness, peeling and sun sensitivity. Reference sources do not describe buffering or slow-ramp schedules specifically, so those practices rest on community and clinician convention rather than the sources reviewed here.

name: Hydrogen water / topical hydrogen

angle.text: Hydrogen water and hydrogen skincare are promoted in wellness and anti-aging circles for antioxidant effects on skin. Users hope for a fresher, younger complexion. The evidence for appearance benefits is thin.

summary: Hydrogen-infused drinks and creams sold on antioxidant claims; the evidence for appearance is thin.
note: Efficacy of hydrogen therapy is described as not established.
currentQuick:
Hydrogen water and hydrogen skincare are marketed as antioxidant anti-ageing products.
Reference sources describe clinical evidence for hydrogen therapy as limited, and none specific to appearance was located.
How it works: Proponents say dissolved H2 reduces oxidative stress and inflammation; this is a proposed mechanism with preliminary support.
Risks and caveats: Safety information was not found in the sources reviewed. Evidence of benefit is limited.
deepLead:
Hydrogen water and topical hydrogen products are drinks and skincare items infused with molecular hydrogen (H2), promoted in some wellness and anti-ageing circles for antioxidant effects on skin and the body.
Wikipedia's article on hydrogen therapy states that its efficacy has not been established, that proposed benefits are linked to reduced oxidative stress and inflammation, and that large-scale clinical evidence is limited. That article does not address hydrogen water products, safety or skin claims specifically.
